title: Injection Technique Evolution: From LoadLibrary to Instrumentation Callbacks
author: dkrasov
summary: A deep dive into how injection techniques have evolved from trivial CreateRemoteThread+LoadLibrary to instrumentation callback abuse, and how Cerberus Layer 1 detects each stage of the progression.
content:
Injection techniques have evolved dramatically over the past decade. The classic CreateRemoteThread + LoadLibrary approach is trivially detected by any modern anti-cheat — it leaves obvious artifacts in the PEB module list and triggers well-known API hooks.

The next evolution was manual mapping: allocating memory via NtAllocateVirtualMemory, copying PE sections manually, resolving imports, and never calling LoadLibrary at all. Advanced variants unlink the allocation from VAD trees and erase PE headers post-load to avoid memory scanners. Cerberus detects this via PTE scanning for executable non-image-backed memory regions — if a page is marked executable but doesn't correspond to a known module on disk, it gets flagged.

Thread hijacking came next — suspending an existing thread via NtCreateThreadEx with THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER, modifying its context to point at injected code, and resuming. No new thread creation means fewer detection surface points. We catch this through thread context change monitoring and stack pivot detection.

Early bird APC injection queues an APC to a thread that hasn't started yet — the payload executes before any user-mode hooks are initialized, including anti-cheat hooks. Our kernel driver monitors APC queue insertions targeting suspended threads and flags pre-initialization execution.

The current frontier is instrumentation callback injection via NtSetInformationProcess(ProcessInstrumentationCallback). This sets a process-wide callback that fires on every kernel-to-user transition, giving the attacker persistent code execution without any thread manipulation. We monitor this by hooking the information class and validating callback registration against known legitimate callers.

Other techniques we track: exception handler hijacking (VEH/SEH chain manipulation to redirect execution flow), and Heaven's Gate — abusing the WoW64 transition layer to execute 64-bit code from a 32-bit process, bypassing 32-bit hooks entirely.

Our current instrumentation callback detection sits at 72% — we're actively expanding coverage for v0.4.3 by adding kernel-level NtSetInformationProcess filtering for the ProcessInstrumentationCallback class. Heaven's Gate detection is at 81% via segment selector monitoring.

title: The DMA Hardware Arms Race: FPGA Boards, Firmware Injection, and Why Device Lists Fail
author: dkrasov
summary: FPGA-based DMA boards, firmware input injection via KMBox, and neural network inference on external hardware represent the next wave of undetectable cheats. Here's what we're seeing and how we're responding.
content:
DMA cheating has moved far beyond off-the-shelf Screamer boards. The current generation uses custom FPGA implementations — Artix-7 based boards with bespoke bitstreams that emulate legitimate PCIe device IDs (Intel NICs, USB controllers, audio devices). Device enumeration is worthless against these because the TLP layer faithfully reproduces the configuration space of real hardware.

The most sophisticated setups use custom FPGA bitstreams with TLP masking — randomizing read patterns, inserting jitter into completion timing, and batching memory reads to mimic legitimate DMA from a network card. Our TLP timing analysis catches the baseline variants (200-800ns latency spikes from PCIe reads), but custom bitstreams with randomized timing are harder — current detection sits at 67%. Each new firmware revision requires building new timing profiles.

The input injection side is equally concerning. KMBox B+ Pro and Arduino Leonardo devices inject HID reports at the firmware level. The USB host controller sees legitimate HID traffic — correct report descriptors, proper polling intervals, valid checksums. From the OS perspective, it's a real keyboard and mouse. Our USB HID polling jitter analysis catches about 44% of known KMBox variants by detecting statistical anomalies in polling interval distributions.

The nightmare scenario — which we're already seeing in the wild — is the full external pipeline: FPGA reads game memory via DMA, sends it to a second PC over high-speed link, the second PC runs an ONNX inference model (typically YOLOv8 fine-tuned on game assets), generates aim corrections, and feeds them back through a KMBox. Zero software footprint on the game PC. No injected code. No modified memory. No suspicious processes.

We're also tracking SPI flash modification for firmware persistence — cheat payloads embedded in NVMe or USB controller firmware that survive OS reinstalls and even drive wipes. Detection requires firmware integrity verification at a level most anti-cheats aren't equipped for.

Our detection approach combines multiple signals: TLP timing profiling, IOMMU attestation (checking for DMA remapping bypass), BAR region analysis (fake devices often have incorrect BAR sizing), and behavioral AI correlation (even if we can't see the cheat software, the player's behavior still shows ML-generated input patterns).

title: Anti-Tamper & Reverse Engineering Resilience: Protecting the Protector
author: nvoronov
summary: Anti-cheat runs on the attacker's machine. Here's how we make reverse engineering Cerberus expensive enough that our weekly update cadence invalidates their work.
content:
Every anti-cheat faces an asymmetric problem: we run on the attacker's machine. They have full control — kernel debuggers, hardware breakpoints, DMA-based memory access. No client-side protection is unbreakable. Our goal isn't perfection; it's raising the cost of reverse engineering so that cheat developers face weeks of work per update, which our weekly release cadence then invalidates.

Code virtualization is our first layer of defense. Unlike off-the-shelf solutions like VMProtect or Themida (which cheat developers have extensive tooling to devirtualize), we use a custom bytecode VM with an instruction set that rotates per build. Each weekly release generates a new virtual ISA — different opcode mappings, different register semantics, different control flow encoding. Existing devirtualization tools break on every update.

Anti-debugging is multi-layered. We detect hardware breakpoints via DR0-DR7 register polling (NtGetContextThread), timing checks via QueryPerformanceCounter and rdtsc to catch single-stepping, NtQueryInformationProcess with ProcessDebugPort and ProcessDebugObjectHandle to detect attached debuggers, and we scan for artifacts of common anti-anti-debug tools like ScyllaHide and TitanHide.

Anti-dump measures prevent memory dumping of our driver and user-mode components. PE headers are erased post-load, IAT entries are replaced with encrypted thunks that resolve at call time, and code sections are encrypted at rest with on-demand decryption — only the currently executing page is in cleartext.

Driver integrity uses runtime self-hashing: critical code sections compute rolling checksums that are validated against server-side attestation. If the hash doesn't match (indicating a patch or hook), the session is flagged. This makes inline hooking of our driver detectable within one scan cycle.

Control flow obfuscation uses custom LLVM passes — control flow flattening converts function structure into state machines, and opaque predicates insert computationally expensive but predetermined branch conditions that confuse static analysis.

No client-side protection is unbreakable. Our goal is raising RE cost so cheat devs face weeks of work per update, which our weekly cadence invalidates. The economics matter more than the technical perfection.

title: How We Detect Humanized Aimbots
author: s.nakamura
summary: Modern aimbots inject noise and jitter to mimic human input. Our TCN-based behavioral engine sees through the disguise by analyzing micro-movement entropy and trigger-timing spectral patterns.
content:
The arms race in aimbot development has shifted. Raw pixel-perfect snapping is trivial to detect — so cheat developers now inject Gaussian noise, random delays, and artificial jitter to make bot-assisted aim look human. Some even use smoothing curves modeled on real player data.

Our behavioral AI layer uses temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) trained on millions of input samples to decompose aim trajectories into frequency components. Human aim has characteristic spectral signatures — correction impulses at 4-8Hz from the neuromuscular system, micro-tremor patterns, and acceleration curves that follow Fitts's Law.

Humanized aimbots fail at the entropy level. Even the best noise injection produces statistically regular patterns when analyzed across a 30-second window. The entropy score of genuine human input is measurably different from synthetic noise overlaid on programmatic corrections.

We also analyze trigger timing — the interval between acquiring a target and firing. Humans exhibit variable reaction times following a log-normal distribution. Aimbots, even with randomized delays, produce timing distributions with detectable artifacts: truncated tails, periodic modes, or correlation with cursor velocity.

Our current humanization bypass detection rate is 94.2% at the 95% confidence threshold, with a 0.14% false positive rate. Every model update improves this as we train on newly observed cheat variants.

title: BYOVD Attacks: Why We Block Vulnerable Driver Exploits
author: dkrasov
summary: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attacks abuse legitimate signed drivers with known exploits to gain kernel access. Cerberus now maintains a blocklist of 340+ vulnerable drivers and blocks them at load time.
content:
BYOVD is one of the most dangerous attack vectors in modern cheating. The attacker doesn't need to write their own kernel driver — they simply load a legitimate, Microsoft-signed driver that contains a known vulnerability, then exploit it to gain ring-0 access.

Popular targets include old versions of hardware monitoring tools, GPU overclocking utilities, and even anti-cheat drivers from other vendors. Because these drivers carry valid signatures, they pass standard code-signing checks.

Cerberus v0.4.1.8b introduced a BYOVD blocklist — currently tracking 340+ known vulnerable drivers by hash and certificate. When our kernel integrity layer detects a blocked driver attempting to load during a game session, the load is denied and the event is flagged.

We also monitor for the behavioral signatures of BYOVD exploitation: unexpected kernel memory mapping, privilege escalation patterns, and syscall table modifications that follow known exploit chains.

This database is updated weekly from our threat research pipeline and cross-referenced with Microsoft's own recommended driver block rules.

title: DMA Timing Analysis: Catching What Device Lists Miss
author: dkrasov
summary: Traditional DMA detection relies on device enumeration. Our timing-based approach detects DMA attacks by measuring memory access latency patterns, catching even unknown hardware.
content:
DMA-based cheats use a second machine connected via PCIe to read game memory externally. Because the cheat runs on entirely separate hardware, traditional client-side anti-cheat is blind to it.

Most anti-cheat vendors that attempt DMA detection rely on device enumeration — maintaining a list of known DMA boards and checking if they're present on the PCIe bus. This fails against custom or modified hardware.

Our approach is different. We measure memory access timing patterns. When an external device reads memory over PCIe, it introduces measurable latency spikes — typically 200-800ns above baseline — in a pattern that correlates with the cheat's polling frequency. By sampling memory access latencies at high resolution during gameplay, we can detect the timing signature of DMA reads regardless of what hardware is performing them.

Combined with IOMMU configuration attestation (detecting if DMA remapping has been disabled or misconfigured), this gives us detection coverage against both known and zero-day DMA hardware.

title: Cheat-Ring Detection: How Network Sentinel Traces Coordinated Abuse
author: ArsenalRX
summary: A single ban led Network Sentinel to uncover a coordinated boosting ring operating across 47 accounts and 3 partner titles.
content:
Last month, a routine ban flagged by our behavioral AI layer led Network Sentinel to uncover a coordinated boosting ring operating across 47 accounts and 3 partner titles.

The initial detection was straightforward — one account showed aim correction speeds 4x faster than their historical average. Our AI flagged it at 97.8% confidence, and the account was banned.

Network Sentinel then performed its post-ban correlation sweep. It matched the banned account's hardware fingerprint fragments against our global database and found 12 other accounts that had played from the same machine within the past 90 days. Behavioral drift analysis showed 8 of those accounts had similar sudden skill jumps within a 48-hour window — consistent with the same cheat being distributed to a group.

Tracing the network signatures further, Sentinel identified a cluster of 47 accounts across 3 game titles that shared overlapping hardware identities, similar behavioral anomalies, and coordinated play schedules. All 47 were banned in a single wave.

This is the kind of detection that's impossible with client-side analysis alone. You need the server-side view to see the connections between accounts, sessions, and titles.

title: False Positive Engineering: How We Maintain 0.14% FP Rate
author: s.nakamura
summary: A detection system is only as good as its false positive rate. Here's how our multi-layer confidence scoring, adaptive thresholds, and manual review pipeline keep innocent players safe.
content:
Every anti-cheat faces the same fundamental tradeoff: aggressive detection catches more cheaters but risks banning innocent players. A single false positive can destroy trust in your game's competitive integrity.

Cerberus approaches this with layered confidence scoring. No single layer can trigger an auto-ban alone. The verdict engine requires corroboration — a kernel anomaly must correlate with behavioral evidence, or a hardware flag must align with network-level data.

Our auto-ban threshold is 95% confidence from the verdict engine. Detections below this enter the manual review queue, where a threat analyst reviews the full session data within 4 hours (Cerberus tier SLA).

We also use adaptive thresholds per game title. A fighting game has legitimately faster input patterns than an RTS. A competitive FPS player's aim correction speed may be 3x faster than a casual player's. Our models account for this by maintaining per-title and per-skill-bracket baselines.

The result: 0.14% false positive rate across all partner titles, with zero confirmed false bans in the last 60 days.
